CHIEF COMPLAINT
Heel pain in the back of the right heel, radiating up into the calf, worse after workouts and on first waking in the morning.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient presents as a new patient to the office with pain in the back of the right heel that extends up into the calf. Pain is typically present after workouts and on first rising in the morning. Morning pain is described as tightness and a sensation of tearing, which eases after about 10 to 15 minutes of walking. Pain recurs after prolonged sitting followed by standing, and after heavy activity. Pain is predominantly on the right side. Patient is training for a triathlon: running about 10 km in the morning, cycling about 45 to 60 minutes at lunchtime, and swimming about 30 to 60 minutes in the evening, five days per week, alternating long run and long bike sessions on weekends, with one rest day. Patient does not stretch and goes slowly until warmed up.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Musculoskeletal: Positive for right posterior heel and calf pain with morning stiffness and pain after activity and prolonged sitting. Left leg pain denied.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Lower extremities: Mild pain with passive toe dorsiflexion on the right. Mild pain with resisted plantarflexion (pushing against examiner) on the right. No pain with calf squeeze bilaterally. Thompson test negative. Significant tenderness to palpation of the right heel and tender along the right Achilles tendon on palpation proximally.
Left lower extremity: No pain on examination.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Achilles tendinitis, right, attributed to overuse from aggressive triathlon training. Plantar fasciitis was considered early in the visit.
- Discontinue training for one to two weeks.
- Ibuprofen (Advil), three tablets every six hours, as an anti-inflammatory.
- Referral for physical therapy, including strengthening and stretching instruction, with a few visits ordered.
- Return visit seven to ten days after the first physical therapy appointment to monitor progress.
- No x-ray indicated at this time.
- If pain persists at ten days without significant change or activity modification, consider more aggressive treatment.
- Patient agreed with the plan.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Followup of chronic problems: depression, hypertension, and status post rotator cuff repair.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Edward is a 59 year old male with a past medical history significant for depression, hypertension, and prior rotator cuff repair who presents for followup of chronic problems. He has not been seen by this provider in a while.

Depression: He reports doing well over the past six months. He sees a counselor once a week and has been swimming at the pool frequently over the summer and fall. He does not feel the need to start medication at this time and knows he can call if he does. He had previously been trying to manage depression with new strategies without medication, as he is already on several medications.

Hypertension: He reports good days and bad days. He takes his medication daily, including Norvasc. He acknowledges occasional dietary indiscretion with burgers, wine, and salt intake. He checks his blood pressure about once a week at a CVS pharmacy kiosk.

Rotator cuff repair: Repair was performed about eight months ago. He has been progressing well with stretching using a yoga ball and is getting stronger. He has progressed from supervised physical therapy to home exercises, which he plans to continue once a week.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies nasal congestion, chest pain, and shortness of breath. Reports intermittent ankle swelling, mainly near the end of the day, which resolves by the next morning. Otherwise, no additional symptoms discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Blood pressure today: 156/94.
Blood pressure readings over the past couple of months have been running high per clinician review.
Heart: Slight 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously documented and considered stable.
Lungs: Clear.
Lower extremities: 1 to 2+ pitting edema bilaterally.
General examination otherwise described as unremarkable.

RESULTS
Labs: Creatinine stable; remainder reviewed as good per clinician.
EKG: Normal. No evidence of coronary artery disease.
Blood pressure readings: Running high over the past couple of months.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Depression: Doing well with current strategies, including counseling, swimming, and good support system. No medication indicated at this time. Patient may call if he wishes to start medication.

2. Hypertension: Not well controlled at this time. Increase Norvasc to 10 mg daily. Order echocardiogram and lipid panel. Reinforce dietary modification with decreased salt intake.

3. Bilateral lower extremity edema, 1 to 2+ pitting: Likely related to dietary salt intake; discussed diet and decreased salt intake.

4. Status post rotator cuff repair: Progressing well. Continue home exercises. No further intervention needed; appears essentially resolved.

Patient has no questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up visit for diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and peripheral vascular disease.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a female, date of birth 03/05/1946, who consented to recording of the visit. She reports she is doing "same, pretty good." She received a letter from the doctor regarding recent lab results showing poorly controlled blood sugars. Her most recent A1c was 9.9. She reports she is still taking glimepiride 2 mg. The doctor instructed her to increase glimepiride to 4 mg twice daily, and the patient states she just filled her prescription (2 mg tablets). She was instructed to take two 2 mg tablets twice daily using her current supply until the new 4 mg prescription is obtained, then take one 4 mg tablet twice daily. She was counseled to watch for hypoglycemia (weakness, shakiness, sweating) and to report it if it occurs.

Diet: Patient reports she avoids pasta and rarely keeps bread in the house. When she has bread, she buys wheat bread, usually two slices in the morning. She occasionally eats peanut butter sandwiches. She reports she drinks no regular soda, drinks club soda and seltzer water, and does not drink plain water. She was advised to reduce the number of bread slices per day.

Eye care: Patient reports up-to-date eye exams and recently received new glasses. She sees Dr. Sanchez at the Optimum Optometrists group on Liberty Road, where she has seen changing providers. She had cataract surgery (described as iodine treatment for her eyes) followed by a one-month recovery period, and then a new prescription was written. She is not happy with the lens in the operated eye; the other eye is good.

Hypertension: Patient reports a home blood pressure reading of 116 a couple of weeks ago. She is taking metoprolol 50 mg once daily, lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide 20/25 mg once daily, and amlodipine 10 mg once daily, and reports taking all of them.

Hyperlipidemia and peripheral vascular disease: Patient is on atorvastatin and reports tolerating it. She reports constant foot pain, leg pain that limits walking, and pain extending up to the hips, which she thinks may be sciatica. She is trying to walk more.

Tobacco: Patient reports she is still smoking and is not ready to quit. She states she will think about it.

Urinary: Patient reports urination is slower due to age but stable. She urinates several times per day and gets up at night occasionally. She notes she tends to drink fluids in the evening.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever and chills.
Neurologic: Denies headaches and dizziness. Reports feet and leg pain as described above.
Eyes: Reports vision is improved after cataract surgery, with dissatisfaction with one lens.
Respiratory: Reports recent cough with congestion; sputum is relatively clear. Denies shortness of breath. Reports cough improved this morning.
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain, pressure, or tightness.
Gastrointestinal: Denies nausea, vomiting, and GI symptoms.
Genitourinary: Reports slower urinary stream, frequent urination, and occasional nocturia as described above.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Carotids normal. Pulses: no bruits noted.
Cardiovascular: Regular rhythm, normal rate, crisp S1 and S2. No murmurs heard.
Respiratory: Lungs clear. No rales or wheezing.
Extremities: No edema. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable bilaterally. Thickened toenails. Mildly dry skin without skin breakdown. Mildly decreased sensation to light touch in the tips of the first and second toes.

RESULTS
Most recent A1c: 9.9 (per visit discussion).
Home blood pressure: 116 systolic (reported a couple of weeks ago).
Office blood pressure today: 140/60 (per doctor's recheck).
Labs: Blood work and kidney function to be checked today; results not available in transcript.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Type 2 diabetes mellitus with suboptimal control (A1c 9.9): Increase glimepiride to 4 mg twice daily. Patient to use current 2 mg tablets, two tablets twice daily, until new 4 mg prescription is filled, then one 4 mg tablet twice daily. Continue metformin. Hypoglycemia precautions reviewed. Labs drawn today. Dietary counseling: reduce bread intake.
2. Hypertension: Office BP 140/60, home readings reportedly better. Continue metoprolol 50 mg daily, lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide 20/25 mg daily, and amlodipine 10 mg daily. Kidney function to be checked today.
3. Hyperlipidemia and peripheral vascular disease: Continue high-dose atorvastatin (Lipitor) to protect the arteries. Leg and hip pain described as relatively stable; patient encouraged to continue walking.
4. Peripheral neuropathy: Mildly decreased sensation in toes. Keep feet moisturized. Medication option discussed if symptoms worsen; patient currently on multiple medications. Patient plans to obtain foot cream.
5. Tobacco use: Patient not ready to quit. Cessation strongly advised; patient will consider it.
6. Cataract surgery follow-up: Patient dissatisfied with one lens; doctor noted laser cleaning may be an option, pending eye provider evaluation. Continue eye care with Dr. Sanchez.
7. Cough with congestion: Lungs clear on exam; cough reported improved.
8. Urinary symptoms: Slower stream and frequency, stable per patient. Evening fluid intake noted.

Follow-up: Return in four months. Labs today.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up after emergency room visit for shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Louis is a 58-year-old male here for follow-up after an emergency room visit. On Saturday, while playing tennis in very hot, humid conditions, he developed shortness of breath after about half an hour, with difficulty breathing. He thought he was having a heart attack and became very nervous. His wife took him to the ER, where evaluation was reportedly unremarkable, but he was very upset. Approximately six hours after returning home, he felt lightheaded and dizzy. He felt fine on Sunday. He reports taking all of his heart failure medications as prescribed and is in touch with his doctor. He reports dietary adherence to a low-salt diet, with occasional dietary indiscretion involving salty and junk foods.
Past history: He had a cataract removed three months ago, with no subsequent vision problems. He had skin cancer removed about five months ago, which has healed well with no problems since.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for shortness of breath and transient lightheadedness and dizziness following the episode on Saturday. Negative for vision problems. Otherwise, no additional symptoms were discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Blood pressure is elevated. Neck is supple. No jugular venous distention noted. Heart has a regular rate and rhythm with no murmur. Lungs have fine bilateral crackles. Trace bilateral lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
ECG: Stable. Shows left ventricular hypertrophy.
Echocardiogram: Left ventricular systolic function is mildly reduced but stable.
Skin biopsy pathology: Reviewed; complete removal and no concerning findings noted.
ER blood pressure: Reportedly elevated.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute exacerbation of heart failure with shortness of breath, likely precipitated by dietary sodium indiscretion with fluid retention. Associated with a history of congestive heart failure and left ventricular hypertrophy. Heart failure is stable on current medication therapy per echocardiogram.
- Prescribe Lasix 80 mg once daily (extra dose).
- Start carvedilol 25 mg twice daily.
- Reinforce low-sodium diet.
- Nurse to see patient today.
2. Elevated blood pressure, noted in clinic and at the ER. To be discussed further.
3. Status post cataract removal, doing well; no medication changes needed.
4. Status post skin cancer removal, pathology reviewed, doing well; no medication changes needed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Lower back injury, approximately four months in duration.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a adult male who presents with lower back pain after injuring his back about four months ago while moving boxes when his son was moving out of a college dorm. Patient is unsure whether this is a pulled muscle. He reports trying physical therapy at his gym without benefit. Patient reports a transient episode at the time of injury in which he felt like he was going to topple over and could not support his upper body weight, with tingling in the toes of the right foot that resolved after about one hour. He reports no recurrence of the tingling or numbness. He notes intermittent sharp lower back pain with turning or rolling over in sleep, which resolves with changing position. He reports weakness in the legs only when carrying heavy objects; otherwise, legs feel relatively normal, though he is nervous about carrying heavy items. He has taken acetaminophen and ibuprofen, with ibuprofen providing slightly better but shorter-lasting relief. He has also tried heat and ice without meaningful benefit. He denies gastrointestinal upset from ibuprofen. He was evaluated at urgent care, where an MRI was recommended; he did not pursue it at that time due to insurance concerns, but now wishes to proceed.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever and chills.
Genitourinary/GI: Denies bladder or bowel dysfunction, incontinence, or urinary retention.
Neurologic: Transient right toe tingling at onset of injury, resolved; no current numbness or tingling. Leg weakness only with heavy lifting.
Musculoskeletal: Intermittent sharp lower back pain with certain positions, as described in HPI.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Afebrile. Blood pressure approximately 117/56. Heart rate 68. SpO2 95% on room air.
Neck: Bony protuberance noted at C5-C6. Nontender to palpation.
Lumbar spine: Nontender to palpation. Decreased flexion and extension. Positive straight leg raise. Paraspinal muscle spasm of the lumbar spine.
Musculoskeletal: Lower extremity strength equal bilaterally.

RESULTS
Lumbar spine X-ray (obtained prior to visit): No acute bony abnormality; no fracture.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Probable acute lumbar disk herniation, based on persistent symptoms and positive straight leg raise. Symptoms began approximately four months ago following lifting injury.
- Order lumbar spine MRI for evaluation of soft tissue structures.
- Continue physical therapy; refer to physical therapist through health system.
- Prescribe meloxicam 15 mg by mouth once daily for pain and inflammation.
- Discussed possible epidural steroid injection if herniation is confirmed; to be addressed at follow-up.
2. Possible cervical arthritis at C5-C6, based on bony protuberance on exam; nontender. No specific plan documented.
- Patient verbalized no questions; agreed with plan.

Right foot pain and swelling after a landscape brick was dropped on the foot yesterday.

His activity level is inconsistent, with exercise a few times a week, and he has a sedentary job. The pain has not affected his job, but he does not want to be as active as before. Social history: Denies cigarette, tobacco, marijuana, vaping, and e-cigarette use. Reports occasional exposure to secondhand smoke when visiting bars with friends; she tries to limit these visits.

Vitals: BP 118/72, HR 58, RR 14, afebrile, SpO2 99% on room air.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up after hospitalization for heart failure.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a female who was hospitalized for heart failure. She reports that her ankles became swollen and would not go down, even when lying down at night. She had difficulty breathing and needed to be propped up in bed to breathe at night. She felt significantly unwell, and after a friend advised her to call for help due to difficulty talking, she called 911. An ambulance took her to the emergency room. The doctor noted blood pressure of 200/90 at that time. The doctor mentioned concern for pneumonia.

Medication adherence: Patient reports she may miss a dose of medication occasionally but tries to take all of them all the time. She has difficulty remembering to take pills. Discussed use of a pill box or phone alarm; patient agreed to try.

Diet: Patient reports eating salty foods, including salt and vinegar potato chips, which she eats at home almost every day. She was advised to stop eating these. Patient is reluctant but agrees she may need to.

Current status: Since discharge, patient reports she is doing better, with less shortness of breath, which she attributes to walking more. She was started on a water pill (Bumex) and reports frequent urination with near incontinence. She was also started on an additional blood pressure medication and reports feeling somewhat better. She has a home blood pressure cuff but has not used it consistently; she plans to use it daily. Patient reports sleeping well with no shortness of breath or sleep problems at home. Denies chest pain.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive: Ankle swelling, orthopnea (needed to prop up to breathe at night), shortness of breath (improving), urinary frequency with near incontinence.
Negative: Chest pain, shortness of breath or sleep disturbance since returning home.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure 128/72. Temperature 98.7. Heart rate 72. Respiratory rate 18. Oxygen saturation 96%.
Neck: No jugular venous distention.
Cardiac: Two out of six systolic ejection murmur, previously heard and stable.
Lungs: Clear bilaterally.
Extremities: Trace lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Echocardiogram reviewed: Preserved ejection fraction of 55%, abnormal diastolic filling, and mild-to-moderate mitral regurgitation.
Blood pressure at emergency presentation: 200/90.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Congestive heart failure: Likely caused by dietary indiscretion and uncontrolled hypertension.
- Continue Bumex 2 mg once daily.
- Continue low-sodium diet and avoid salty foods.
- Keep a log of blood pressures and food intake, especially if blood pressure is elevated.
- Weigh daily; call if weight gain of 3 pounds in 2 days.
- Referral to nutritionist for dietary education.

2. Hypertension: Uncontrolled prior to admission.
- Continue Cozaar 100 mg daily.
- Continue Norvasc 5 mg once daily.
- Order renal artery ultrasound to evaluate for possible renal artery stenosis.
- Home blood pressure monitoring with cuff, daily use.
- Medication adherence strategies: pill box or phone alarm.

3. Kidney disease: Labs to be ordered to monitor tolerance of new medications.

Follow-up in 3 months.

Patient had no further questions.

Julie is a patient referred by her primary care doctor for bilateral knee pain of about six months' duration. She believes it could be tendonitis. She cannot recall any specific precipitating event, fall, or injury. The pain is located right behind the kneecaps and is described as deep and achy. It is worsened by standing up after sitting for a while, by going up and down stairs, and by movement from a sitting position. The pain improves after a period of activity. She has tried ibuprofen or naproxen (Aleve) and acetaminophen (Tylenol) as needed, which take the edge off, but she is not pain-free except when resting. She works from home; her office is downstairs except for a morning trip upstairs. She is a runner who previously ran five to six miles daily but now can barely run half a mile due to knee pain. She has never injured or broken a bone.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for redness and swelling of the knees. Positive for bilateral knee pain as described above. Otherwise, not discussed.

RESULTS
Bilateral knee X-rays: no fractures or osteoarthritis.

- Referral to physical therapy for lower extremity exercises to increase strength and mobility and to correct any running mechanics issues.
- Activity should be modified for now; a gradual return to running is anticipated.

He denies waking up short of breath this time; this occurred six months ago but not in the current episode. He last saw his nephrologist about one month ago. He has stage 3 chronic kidney disease. He reports taking ibuprofen (Motrin) about one week ago for foot pain and stopped as quickly as he could. He reports Tylenol is not very effective for his pain. He reports one episode of foot pain in the area just in front of the big toe of one foot, lasting four to five days and then slowly resolving. He has no known prior history of gout.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Tacrolimus ointment was selected as an alternative to cream, to be sent to Metro Market pharmacy.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right foot pain following a tennis injury approximately a couple of days ago.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a right-handed individual who presents with right foot pain after injuring the foot while playing doubles tennis. While attempting to volley the ball, she got in front of another player and fell on top of her right foot, then twisted to try to catch herself, after which she felt pain in the foot. She could not continue playing and had to be helped off the field because she could not bear weight on the foot. Since the injury she has wrapped the foot with an ACE wrap, applied ice, kept it elevated on a pillow, and taken ibuprofen, which helps a little but wears off after a while. The injury occurred about a couple of days ago. Patient reports a prior injury to her left foot; no prior injury to the right foot was reported. Patient denies numbness and reports no loss of sensation. Patient self-reports a possible bone bruise.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for numbness and loss of sensation in the right foot. Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 125/70. Respiratory rate 18. Temperature 97.1. Oxygen saturation 100%. Pulse approximately 60 beats per minute.
Cardiovascular: No murmur, rub, or gallop. Regular rate and rhythm.
Respiratory: Mild stridor noted. No wheezes or rales.
Abdomen: No rebound or guarding.
Skin: Not discussed in detail beyond general statement that patient does not feel hot to touch.
HEENT/General: Head symmetrical. Mucous membranes normal.
Right foot: Bruising of the plantar and dorsal aspects. Swelling at the midfoot. Tenderness to palpation of the midfoot. Positive piano key test of the first and second metatarsals. Warm to touch.
Right foot neurovascular: Capillary refill less than 3 seconds. Strong dorsalis pedis pulse. Sensation intact to light touch.
Left foot: Normal exam. Capillary refill appropriate, pedal pulses strong, sensation intact to light touch.

RESULTS
Right foot X-ray (reviewed by physician): Subtle dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal, 3 mm separation of the first and second metatarsal bases, and a bony fragment in the Lisfranc joint space.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right foot pain consistent with Lisfranc fracture involving the second metatarsal base, based on exam and X-ray findings.
- Surgical intervention recommended to realign bones using plates and screws and to prevent complications such as poor bone alignment, poor ligament healing, loss of the foot arch (flatfoot), and arthritis.
- MRI ordered to further assess the fracture and any ligamentous injury.
- Day surgery planned; patient will need a driver to take her home.
- Post-operative follow-up in clinic in about one week. Cast and crutches; non-weight-bearing on the right foot for six to eight weeks, then gradual weight-bearing as tolerated based on progress.
- Physical therapy recommended after surgery to strengthen muscles and prepare for return to play.
- Patient informed she will be out for the rest of the tennis season.
- Surgical risks (including bleeding, loss of sensation, and nerve damage) to be reviewed with patient via paperwork provided, with explanation by medical assistant. Patient encouraged to ask questions before and after the procedure.

Evaluation of abnormal renal ultrasound with an atrophic right kidney.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Ashley James is a 14-year-old female, previously healthy, referred for evaluation of an abnormal renal ultrasound showing an atrophic right kidney. Per family, Ashley developed acute right-sided abdominal pain, bent over in pain, initially suspected to be appendicitis or kidney stone. She was seen by her physician and treated for a presumed stomach virus with fluids and discharged, then returned the next day worse. Repeat testing (family believes an ultrasound) showed one kidney was larger. A follow-up with her primary care physician was brief and she continued to have vomiting and pain. She was evaluated in Jacksonville, where the right kidney was described as atrophic and much smaller than the left, and non-functional per their assessment. Imaging reportedly also showed cysts on the kidney and ovaries and possibly other sites, swollen lymph nodes, and an infection. Family was advised to follow up with the primary physician, who was out of town. The family then came to Atlanta, where she was seen and treated over about four days. Vomiting has resolved, but she continues to have abdominal pain and a burning sensation, especially with eating. Per family, she had no problems before this episode, though they believe she may have had a severe infection that affected her kidney. At age four she had three or four hospitalizations, sometimes lasting three days, for recurrent fever and symptoms treated with fluids and antibiotics without documented infectious workup; this recurred over a couple of months and then stopped. Family is seeking evaluation and, if needed, management including possible removal of the kidney.

Current symptoms: Reports mild abdominal pain and burning. Reports sometimes difficulty initiating urination. Denies noticed blood in urine. Family reports burning with urination when drinking carbonated beverages; she drinks only Gatorade or water.

Medications: Famotidine (Pepcid) 40 mg daily; loratadine (Claritin) for allergies.

Pregnancy/delivery history: No difficulties reported with the patient's pregnancy or delivery with Ashley.

Family history: Renal disease in the father (kidney transplant; obstructive neuropathy per discussion), paternal aunt (diagnoses reported as end-stage renal disease, CKD stage 5, diabetes, hypertension; adult onset), and cousins with kidney issues; family provided records. Father died at age 47 of a massive heart attack per family; later discussion indicated he was dialysis-dependent at the time of death, with posterior urethral valves and obstructive neuropathy noted in grandfather's record. Mother had breast cancer. Ashley has seen GI and genetics; panel showed no clinically significant mutations.

Social history: Active in softball; plans to join a drill team over the summer.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for abdominal pain, burning sensation, and dysuria-related hesitancy. Negative for hematuria per patient. Positive for burning with carbonated drinks per family. Vomiting has resolved. Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Heart: Normal. Lungs: Normal.
General: Well-appearing female, alert and oriented, sitting comfortably, not in acute distress.
Remainder of exam: Within normal limits.

RESULTS
Renal ultrasound: Atrophic right kidney, smaller than left; left kidney appears enlarged (per outside records and discussion).
Renal function: Described as good per physician review.
Blood pressure: Described as good.
Genetics/GI: Panel without clinically significant mutations.
Outside imaging/findings reported by family: cysts on kidney and ovaries, possible other sites, swollen lymph nodes, infection (not independently reviewed in visit).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Atrophic right kidney with compensatory left kidney enlargement. Kidney function and blood pressure currently appear good. Ashley is at increased risk for hypertension and proteinuria. No intervention needed today; monitor.
 - Annual renal ultrasound to monitor kidney size and function.
 - Annual urinalysis to monitor for protein and blood.
 - Annual blood pressure check.
2. Abdominal pain and dysuria-type symptoms. Likely sensitivity related to carbonated beverages per physician discussion.

4. Lifestyle: Continue healthy diet and active lifestyle. Family reports already eating well.
5. Follow-up: Next appointment with primary care physician or an adult nephrologist closer to home. Family to call with questions or if symptoms worsen.
6. Family history: Physician to review family-provided records for father, aunt, and cousins.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up after hospitalization at District Regional Hospital (admitted 06/29/2021, discharged 07/02/2021) for fever, elevated white blood cell count, spasms, lightheadedness, constipation, diaphoresis, labile blood pressure, headache, and vomiting. Patient also requests discussion regarding COVID-19 vaccination.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 39-year-old female (DOB 05/07/1982) with quadriplegia due to prior spinal cord injury and a suprapubic catheter. She was admitted to District Regional Hospital on 06/29/2021 with increasing spasms and lightheadedness, significant constipation, and diaphoresis. In the emergency department she was febrile with a white blood cell count of 23,000, and there were concerns for urinary tract infection; she was treated with IV antibiotics. She also had labile blood pressure, headache, and vomiting. She improved slowly and was discharged on 07/02/2021 after clinical improvement. Cultures were obtained and reviewed.

Patient does not believe the illness was a urinary tract infection. She feels her blood pressure was elevated due to constipation; she had hardly had a bowel movement while hospitalized and felt much better after a large bowel movement at home. Patient wondered whether automatic dysreflexia can affect white blood cell count. Doctor noted that dysreflexia typically does not affect white count, that the urine cultures were not very impressive, and that her white count was normal last year but is mildly elevated now, which can occur with inflammation or bowel backup. Hospital imaging was an x-ray only; no CT was performed. Patient reports she is now back to her normal self. She went to the hospital because her blood pressure was out of control, with headache and vomiting, and she could not manage at home.

Patient takes MiraLAX daily and doubles up when she does not have a bowel movement. She has lactulose at home as a rescue medication, which takes about two days to work.

Doctor raised the possibility of a pressure sore. Doctor attributed some of the presentation to dehydration from a period of extreme heat, noting that she has been staying indoors more during hot weather.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient reports no pain or discomfort anywhere. Patient reports she is otherwise doing well. Constipation as described in the history of present illness. No other systems discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Cardiopulmonary examination performed; patient instructed to take deep breaths and breathe normally. Patient denies pain or discomfort. No other findings documented.

RESULTS
Hospital white blood cell count 23,000 (elevated). Urine cultures reviewed by physician and described as not very impressive. Hospital imaging: x-ray only; no CT performed. No other results discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute-on-chronic constipation. Patient believes her hospitalization was more likely due to autonomic dysreflexia related to her quadriplegia, with blood pressure fluctuations, and that her constipation was the primary driver rather than a true urinary tract infection. Patient has a reasonable bowel regimen (daily MiraLAX, lactulose as rescue). Possible contributing factors include dehydration during hot weather.
Plan: Return in two to three weeks for fasting labs, including complete blood count with differential to recheck white blood cell count and a full lipid panel (cholesterol panel, due given time since last check). If white count remains elevated, further evaluation of bowel issues would be considered.

2. Leukocytosis, resolved status unknown. White count was normal last year and elevated during hospitalization. Possibly inflammation or backed-up bowel. Plan: repeat CBC as above.

3. Quadriplegia due to prior spinal cord injury. Possible pressure sore was raised by physician; no examination findings documented. Plan: Not discussed further.

4. COVID-19 vaccination status: unvaccinated. Patient has concerns about unknown side effects, reports of "vaccine injury," and feels she is young and healthy. Patient also takes vitamin C and multivitamins. Physician recommended vaccination, stating she is high risk given quadriplegia, that the vaccine is the only proven preventive measure, and that supplements are not expected to prevent COVID-19. Physician discussed rare vaccine side effects, including Guillain-Barre syndrome. Patient is open-minded and will think about it. Patient was encouraged to ask further questions.

Follow-up: two to three weeks with labs as above.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
New right eye twitch.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Karen Nelson is a 3-year-old female with no significant past medical history who presents with her father for evaluation of a new right eye twitch. Father noticed the twitch a couple of weeks ago and was advised by the pediatrician to come in. Karen reports sensing the twitch in her face at times, with an urge to move her face that is relieved once the movement occurs. She reports no pain with the episodes. Father reports the twitch occurs several times an hour on some days and is absent on other days, sometimes not appearing until late afternoon. He has observed it daily for the past several weeks. Per father, the whole side of the face moves during episodes, lasting several seconds, followed by frequent blinking. Karen continues her activities during episodes. Father reports she otherwise seems well, eating well, playing with friends, and carrying out normal activities. Father has not observed other body parts moving or twitching. Father has made a video of an episode, which was offered for review. No history of seizures in Karen. No family history of seizures or Tourette syndrome. Family members have no similar history.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for fever and chills. Negative for sleep problems. Cough and headache were asked about; the patient's response was unclear and not documented. No other symptoms discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neurological exam: Patient awake, alert, and oriented x3. Speech clear and fluent. Gait steady, heel-toe walking normal. Cranial nerves intact without focal neurologic findings. No pronator drift. Sensation intact, including testing with eyes closed. Reflexes 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, knees, and ankles. Patient followed finger movements with eyes and performed commands during examination.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right eye twitch, most consistent with a tic. Discussed that tics are common in children, with about one in five children having a tic during school years. Tics are brief, sudden, involuntary motor movements and can include shoulder shrugging, facial grimacing, sniffling, throat clearing, or vocalizations. Cause is not fully understood. Tics typically begin around ages 5 to 10 and most are transient, resolving within a year. Plan is to ignore the tic, as drawing attention to it may make it worse. Symptoms may wax and wane and may be more noticeable when tired or stressed. Seizure considered unlikely given that the same body part moves each time, the urge and relief pattern, and normal neurological exam. No medication or topical treatment recommended at this time, as Karen is doing well overall and the tic has not affected school or activities. Treatment will be considered if symptoms worsen. Father's questions were addressed. Follow-up as needed if worsening.

Her depression has good and bad days, with some days feeling extremely low; she is still taking Effexor. Overall physical exam is within normal limits except for mild wheezes in all lung fields.

Pulmonary function tests: suggest possible asthma or COPD.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Return visit for irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) with functional abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Ms. Brittany Edwards is a pleasant 32-year-old female last seen in August 2019 for flares of abdominal pain. She was diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome and treated with Bentyl. She previously received a prescription for Reglan from the emergency room, which she used as needed for nausea. At the prior visit, she was instructed to start a low-dose daily fiber supplement such as Citrucel, daily probiotics for gas and bloating, Bentyl up to four times daily for intestinal cramping, and to stop Reglan and use Zofran as needed. Neuromodulators such as Elavil and Buspar were discussed but not started.

Since the last visit, the patient reports feeling "not so good." She has been eating out on Friday and Saturday nights, including spicy foods and spicy shrimp. She reports experiencing both lower abdominal symptoms (cramping) and upper abdominal symptoms (nausea). She suspects possible lactose intolerance. Her normal bowel movement frequency is two to three times daily, with formed stools. She tends to have more diarrhea after going out drinking with friends. She usually orders chicken alfredo at a restaurant, which she reports normally does not bother her. Her typical alcohol choices are tequila, dark liquor (Patron, or two brown liquors), and occasionally a martini. She has not had success using Citrucel regularly. She reports ongoing cramping and sharp pains during the week and has been avoiding heavy foods. She ate fried chicken today and reports she was fine for the most part. She has been drinking water instead of sodas with some improvement.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Alert and cooperative, appears stated age.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm.
Respiratory: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender. No masses or organomegaly. Normal active bowel sounds.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Irritable bowel syndrome with functional abdominal pain, aggravated by dietary triggers (spicy, fatty, and dairy-containing foods, alcohol, and sugary mixers), high stress, poor eating habits, and poor sleep habits.
- Start Citrucel (fiber) tablet twice daily for regularity.
- Bentyl (dicyclomine) 20 mg as needed: take one tablet 30 to 45 minutes before leaving the house for restaurant meals and a second tablet at the restaurant, repeating up to four times daily as needed for cramping. Refill provided.
- Start Elavil (amitriptyline) 25 mg nightly at bedtime as a neuromodulator to reduce visceral sensitivity and help prevent flares. Counseled that it may cause sleepiness.
- Encouraged dietary and lifestyle modifications, including reducing greasy and fatty foods, sugary drinks, and alcohol, watching portion sizes, and identifying food patterns that worsen symptoms.
- Continue to stay well hydrated with water.
- Patient may use Zofran as needed for nausea; advised not to take it prophylactically and to drink plenty of water.
- Prescriptions sent to pharmacy.
2. Follow-up: Patient to check in via MyChart email in about one month regarding symptoms, side effects, or medication adjustments.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right index finger pain, swelling, and limited motion following a hyperextension injury in a motor vehicle accident in March of this year. Patient seeking a second opinion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 50-year-old male (DOB 1/12/71) who presents for a second opinion regarding the right index finger. He was a passenger in a car that was rear-ended multiple times in March of this year. He felt two bumps that propelled him forward and stretched the right index finger, and he believes the finger went backward; he is unsure whether it dislocated. Since the injury he reports persistent pain and swelling, inability to make a fist, and pain severe enough at times to be unbearable, including with driving.

Prior care: He was offered an injection of the A1 pulley region at his prior orthopedic evaluation but declined steroid because of a reaction to dexamethasone (causes his heart to race). He was scheduled to see Dr. Alice Davis but apparently did not attend. He was evaluated at Point May Orthopedics, largely by physical therapy staff and a PA. An MRI was obtained for concern of capsular strain plus or minus rupture of the FDS tendon. He has since been treated with occupational therapy, which has been limited by pain. Per the patient, he was told an injection was not advised because it could worsen the tear, and he has been instructed to avoid rubbing the finger and performing hand activities. He feels he is not receiving adequate care.

Occupation and social: He is right-handed and works as an X-ray technician. He reports he drove himself to this visit.

Medications and allergies: Takes a blood pressure medication. Denies diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. Reports itching with methylprednisolone. Reaction to dexamethasone noted as above.

Patient reports he has not had therapy scheduled or set up at this time. He has purchased a splint on his own.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for right index finger pain, swelling, stiffness, numbness over the finger, and inability to make a fist. Negative for diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis per patient. Otherwise not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Pleasant, cooperative, healthy-appearing male in no distress.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; 2+ radial pulse.
Right hand: No swelling or bruising noted, except bruising in the palm over the volar surface of the index finger. Normal creases. Slightly diminished prominence over the PIP of the index finger compared with the middle finger. Index finger rests in a 10-degree PIP flexed position.
Tenderness: Tender with pressure over the index finger area; less tender at a second site; patient reports mild numbness.
Range of motion: Active flexion of the index finger was performed with the patient reporting significant pain and a sensation of tearing. Patient unable to make a full fist. Pain reported with flexion at the MCP region.

RESULTS
Right hand X-rays (four views, today): No bony abnormalities. Joint congruency throughout all lesser digits of the right hand. No concerning soft tissue shadows. No arthritis.

Outside MRI of right index finger (4/24/2021, Point May Orthopedics, as summarized by physician): Focal soft tissue swelling over the right index MCP joint; partial-thickness tear of the right FDS tendon; fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around the FDP and FDS tendons. Radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of the index MCP joint intact; MCP joint capsule intact; extensor tendons intact.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Post-traumatic, rather severe stenosing tenosynovitis of the right index finger, with partial-thickness tear of one half of the FDS tendon (the less important flexor), secondary scar tissue and inflammation around the FDS impeding excursion of the FDP and FDS tendons through the pulley system. Collateral ligaments and extensor tendons intact. Stiffness and pain are the main issues; the FDP is intact.

Plan:
1. Right index finger trigger injection with betamethasone (Celestone) today, avoiding dexamethasone given prior reaction. Procedure note: First attempt with 1 cc Celestone and 0.5 cc lidocaine was not completed due to a sudden, marked pain reaction with hand contortion and patient withdrawing the hand; needle withdrawn. Patient counseled on the importance of getting steroid into the flexor tendon sheath. Second attempt using the same technique with 1 cc Celestone and 0.5 cc lidocaine. A small palmar vein bled a scant amount; cleaned and bandaged. Patient reassured that no harm was done to the finger. Post-procedure instructions: ice the finger this evening and take ibuprofen.
2. Expected improvement in three to five days, with further improvement over the next couple of weeks. Repeat injection may be needed.
3. Outpatient occupational/physical therapy once a week for six weeks, with the goal of full active and passive range of motion without restrictions. Patient to return to his prior therapy providers, with weekly check-in for accountability. Outpatient prescription provided.
4. Active motion of the finger is encouraged; splinting is not recommended as it immobilizes the finger. Patient counseled that the finger is stiff and sore and will not be torn further by active movement, since extensor tendons and collateral ligaments are intact.
5. Patient is cleared to drive.

Index finger rests in 10-degree PIP flexion. Tenderness on palpation over the index finger, with less discomfort at a second site. Patient reports numbness over the index finger with palpation. Active flexion of the index finger is limited and painful; patient reports a sensation of tearing with attempted flexion. Pain with flexion at the MCP region.

RESULTS
Right hand x-rays (four views, today): No bony abnormalities. Joint congruency throughout all lesser digits. No concerning soft tissue shadows. No arthritis.

MRI right index finger (4/24/2021, outside facility): Focal soft tissue swelling over the right index MCP joint. Partial-thickness tear of the right flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS). Fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around the FDP and FDS tendons. Radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of the index MCP joint intact. MCP joint capsule intact. Extensor tendons intact.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Post-traumatic, rather severe stenosing tenosynovitis of the right index finger, with partial-thickness tear of one slip of the FDS tendon. The FDP is intact. Collateral ligaments and extensor tendons are intact. Likely scar tissue and inflammation around the FDS are impairing excursion of the flexor tendons through the pulley.

Plan:
1. Right index finger trigger finger (A1 pulley) steroid injection performed today with betamethasone (Celestone), 1 cc, with 0.5 cc lidocaine. Avoid dexamethasone given prior reaction. Patient had a significant pain reaction with the first needle attempt, and the needle was withdrawn. A second attempt was made using the same technique. A small palmar vein bled a scant amount; this was cleaned and a bandage was applied. Patient reassured that no harm was done to the finger. Post-procedure instructions: ice the finger this evening and take ibuprofen.
2. Expected improvement in pain over 3 to 5 days, with further improvement over the next couple of weeks. Repeat injection may be needed.
3. Outpatient occupational or physical therapy once a week for six weeks, with a goal of full active and passive range of motion without restrictions. Patient to check in weekly with the therapy team for accountability. Continue active motion of the finger; splint use is not recommended as it immobilizes the finger.
4. Counseled that the finger is stiff and sore but that there is no risk of tearing or breaking a bone with active motion, since the extensor tendons and collateral ligaments are intact.
5. Patient is cleared to drive.
6. Follow up as needed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Bilateral hand numbness and tingling.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Shirley Taylor, DOB 5/4/1961, MRN 0000123, is a 60-year-old right-handed female, new patient, referred by Dr. Jacob Ward for evaluation of bilateral hand numbness and tingling. The patient reports numbness and tingling in both hands for a few weeks. She believes it may be a pinched nerve. Symptoms began after a car accident last December in which she broke both wrists; she notes the tingling and numbness became more noticeable as her wrists healed. Both hands have worsened over the last month. The right side is worse. She wears a splint on the right wrist, which seems to help, and sometimes wears the left splint as well. Her wrists were more painful at the time of the injury than they are today.

Right hand: numbness and tingling from the middle and ring fingers up to the forearm.
Left hand: numbness and tingling mainly in the pinky and ring fingers, not the middle finger.

Symptoms are mainly soreness, sometimes throbbing. Hands feel weaker, especially with use. Tingling occurs more at night and comes and goes throughout the day. When the hands hurt, the tingling subsides and then becomes dull. The patient describes her hands as possibly less sensitive than they should be, but she can still feel. She denies loss of sensation. She was prescribed nerve pain medication but has not been taking it as directed.

She also reports mild neck stiffness. She hit her head during the accident and was told she had a contusion.

Past medical history per chart review: chronic kidney disease, gout, hypertension, anxiety, GERD, and diabetes. The patient reports prior pre-diabetes, now controlled through diet. Current medications include carvedilol 25 mg twice daily for hypertension and Lexapro 10 mg daily for anxiety; she confirms adherence. Allergy: sulfa drugs (causes rash). No history of thyroid disease.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: fatigue, weight gain.
GI: excessive appetite, bloating.
Eyes: floaters.
Cardiovascular: shortness of breath, leg swelling.
Endocrine: positive for diabetes; always hungry.
Skin: nail bed trenches, dryness, itching.
Musculoskeletal: gout, muscle pain.
Neurological: paresthesia, bilateral hands.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neurological exam:
Sensation normal except pinprick sensation diminished in the third and fourth fingers on the right and the fourth and fifth fingers on the left.
Reflexes 1+ and symmetric; 2+ at the knees. Toes downgoing bilaterally.
Tinel's sign positive at both wrists and both elbows.

RESULTS
CT brain with and without contrast (2/5/21), personally reviewed by the physician: no metastatic disease, no acute intracranial abnormalities.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome.
2. Question of bilateral cubital tunnel syndrome.

Impression discussed with the patient. Plan:
- Schedule EMG and nerve conduction velocity (NCV) studies.
- If symptoms do not resolve, consider hand clinic referral for possible symptomatic injections or carpal tunnel release surgery. These may also be pursued through her current orthopedist.
- Encouraged continued use of wrist splints.
- Return for EMG/NCV.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Evaluation of kidney stones, referred by primary care physician.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient presents for evaluation of kidney stones after a referral from his PCP. Approximately one week ago, while working in the barn moving hay, he developed sudden onset of right back pain. He initially attributed the pain to lifting but then became diaphoretic and nauseated, prompting a visit to his PCP. A CT scan was ordered and showed a kidney stone. He has no prior personal history of kidney stones; his father has had kidney stones. The pain radiated from the right back to near the groin. He has had no pain since that initial episode, apart from a couple of brief recurrences after the diagnosis, which were shorter in duration. He has been straining his urine as instructed and has not seen any stone material. He has not noticed blood in his urine or darker urine than usual.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive: Right back pain radiating toward the groin, diaphoresis, nausea, intermittent brief recurrences of pain.
Negative: Hematuria, dark urine. Fever was not reported; the doctor noted no fever on vitals.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs reported as within normal limits (no fever; blood pressure and heart rate described as normal).
Abdomen: Nontender to palpation. No rebound or guarding.
Costovertebral angle: Tenderness on the right side.

RESULTS
CT scan (reviewed by physician): Stone measuring 0.5 cm in the proximal right ureter. No evidence of hydronephrosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right proximal ureteral kidney stone (0.5 cm), without hydronephrosis. Right CVA tenderness consistent with the stone.
- Increase oral fluid intake to facilitate urination and passage of the stone.
- Prescribe oxycodone 5 mg every 6 to 8 hours for pain. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) may be taken between doses for breakthrough pain.
- Continue straining urine; patient already has a strainer.
- Order basic metabolic panel (BMP), urinalysis, and urine culture. Antibiotics to be prescribed based on urinalysis results if infection is identified.
- Follow-up in 1 to 2 weeks to assess for stone passage. If the stone has not passed, further treatment will be discussed, including lithotripsy (extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy, a non-invasive procedure that breaks up the stone).
- Nurse to send in prescription.

He states it may be lactose intolerance but is not sure. He was seen in the ER a few months ago and had an abdominal CT, which the patient reports showed nothing significant; the referring physician reviewed the report and confirms it was normal. Over the past couple of months he has noted alternating constipation and diarrhea. Previously his bowel movements were normal.

Constipation: He is more often constipated than has diarrhea. He usually does not have a bowel movement, and when he does the stool is hard. Bowel movements occur about three to four times per week when constipated. Abdominal pain improves somewhat after a bowel movement.

Diarrhea: Occurs intermittently, depending on diet. He reports a sensitive stomach and states that creamy pasta sauces trigger diarrhea. Episodes are usually single and self-limited.

Denies blood in the stool. Weight is stable, though he would like to lose about 25 pounds.

Family history: Sister has irritable bowel syndrome. Patient believes he may have IBS but has never been diagnosed. No family history of GI cancer or liver disease.

Surgical history: No abdominal surgeries. Gallbladder and appendix intact.

Colonoscopy: Never performed.

Medications: Rosuvastatin (Crestor) daily for about 18 months, olmesartan daily, and acetaminophen (Tylenol) for occasional pain, about once a month.

Social history: Drinks a couple of beers on Saturdays after yard work. No history of heavy alcohol or drug use.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for nausea, vomiting, heartburn, and indigestion. Eating and drinking adequately. Negative for blood in stool, easy bruising or bleeding, and ankle or foot swelling. Weight stable. Positive for constipation, intermittent diarrhea, and intermittent abdominal pain as described above.

Pulmonary: Lungs clear bilaterally.

- Constipation with increased stool burden; likely diet-related diarrhea. Physician does not think hepatomegaly explains GI symptoms.

Numbness and tingling in both hands for a few weeks. Referred for evaluation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 60-year-old right-handed male (MRN abc123, DOB January 1, 1960) referred for evaluation of numbness and tingling in both hands for a few weeks. He attributes onset to a car accident last December in which he broke both wrists. He notes the symptoms became more noticeable after the fractures healed, and both sides have worsened over the last month, with the right worse than the left. He wears a splint on the right wrist and sometimes on the left; the splint helps. He reports mild neck stiffness and hit his head during the accident, at which time he was told he had a contusion.

Symptoms are on the right from the middle and ring fingers up the forearm, and on the left from the pinky and ring fingers up the forearm. He describes mainly soreness, intermittent throbbing, and a sensation of weakness, especially with use. Tingling increases when the hands hurt and is dull when it resolves. Symptoms are worse at night and come and go during the day. He reports hands may be less sensitive than expected but denies loss of the ability to feel touch. He was prescribed nerve pain medication but has not been taking it as directed.

Current medications include Coreg for hypertension and Lexapro for anxiety. History of prediabetes, now controlled with diet. No history of thyroid disease.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: fatigue, weight gain.
GI: excessive appetite, bloating.
Eyes: floaters.
Cardiovascular: shortness of breath, leg swelling.
Endocrine: always hungry.
Skin: nail bed changes, dryness, itching.
Musculoskeletal: gout, muscle pain.
All other systems negative per patient confirmation.

Neurologic examination:
Sensation: Pinprick diminished in the third and fourth fingers on the right and in the fourth and fifth fingers on the left. Otherwise normal.

Tinel sign: positive at both wrists and both elbows, with radiating symptoms reported on percussion.
Remainder of exam normal.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

- Order EMG/nerve conduction study to localize the nerve involvement and assess nerve responsiveness.
- Continue wearing wrist splints.
- Follow-up visit after testing is completed.
- If symptoms persist, consider referral to hand clinic for injections or carpal tunnel release surgery, or referral to orthopedics for the same treatment.
2. Neuropathic symptoms: nerve pain medication was prescribed; the patient has not been taking it as directed. Adherence was not specifically addressed in the plan.
3. Hypertension and anxiety: continue Coreg and Lexapro per patient report.
4. Prediabetes, controlled with diet per patient report.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Jordan Roberts is a 49-year-old man with hypertension and palpitations, presenting as a new patient. He was recently seen in the emergency room with high blood pressure and palpitations, which he reports occurred in March. On that day he had several cups of coffee and no breakfast; he believes the episode was more likely a panic attack. The doctor raised the possibility of low blood sugar. He has not had recurrent palpitations since.

He reports blood pressure problems since childhood and a family history of hypertension. He felt his blood pressure was improving until about one month ago, when his new primary care physician started him on a combination medication, Benicar HCT (olmesartan/hydrochlorothiazide, 40-25). He is also taking amlodipine 10 mg daily.

He checks his blood pressure at home every morning, with readings of approximately 146 to 155 mmHg lately. He has not yet reached the 120s. He reports reducing salt intake and not eating excessive salt. He tries to walk on a treadmill when able.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for palpitations in the past, none recently. Positive for dizziness is not reported. No other systems discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Patient ambulatory and conversant.
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds normal per physician.
Respiratory: Lungs normal per physician.
Abdomen: Palpated; patient reported no tenderness.
Extremities: Ankles and feet examined for swelling; no swelling noted.
Vital signs: Not discussed.

RESULTS
Potassium one week prior: 4.0. Repeat potassium not obtained in the past week.
Thyroid profile from March 1, 2021: referenced for copy-forward; results not discussed.
Home blood pressure readings: approximately 146 to 155 mmHg, every morning.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Resistant hypertension. Patient is on three antihypertensive medications at maximum dose (amlodipine 10 mg daily, Benicar HCT 40-25, with hydrochlorothiazide component) with blood pressure still elevated. The physician suspects a secondary cause, possibly hyperaldosteronism, given onset at a young age and failure to respond to three agents.
- Start spironolactone.
- Counseled on risks: electrolyte disturbances (including hyponatremia and hyperkalemia), dehydration and dizziness on standing, and gynecomastia (about 1 in 100 men). Patient should stop the medication and notify the physician if gynecomastia develops.
- Metabolic panel (potassium and sodium) and blood pressure check in two weeks.
- Hydration counseling provided.
